mcqs.question: A policy document states "only finance can see salary data." Why does this alone not actually protect the data?
options: Policy documents are legally binding and therefore automatically enforced by the warehouse
Salary data cannot be stored in a data warehouse under any circumstances
Finance teams are never granted database access in any organization
The policy does nothing on its own — someone has to implement the actual row/column security rule that enforces it, and keep it correct as new pipelines, reports, or exports are built
mcqs.explanation: A policy statement has no mechanical effect on a database — actual enforcement requires someone to implement and maintain the specific access rule, and to ensure new pipelines don't create side doors around it. Policy documents are not automatically enforced by any warehouse mechanism, salary data is routinely and legitimately stored in warehouses, and finance teams are commonly granted appropriate access.

mcqs.question: Why is PII classification done systematically (automated detection plus review, recorded as metadata) rather than relying on engineers remembering which columns are sensitive?
options: Automated detection is the only method capable of finding any sensitive column, making manual review entirely unnecessary

Manual memory doesn't survive organizational turnover or scale to thousands of columns, and recording classification as shared metadata means every downstream rule references the same source instead of each team re-deciding independently
PII classification is only required once per year, so memory-based tracking is sufficient
Systematic classification is purely a legal requirement with no practical engineering benefit
mcqs.explanation: Relying on memory fails predictably as people leave and schemas grow, while shared, recorded classification gives every access-control rule and every team the same consistent answer. Automated detection alone misses less obvious cases that need human review, classification isn't a once-a-year exercise given how frequently schemas change, and it has real, immediate engineering value beyond legal compliance.

mcqs.question: What's the defining feature of row-level and column-level security compared to relying on report authors to write correct WHERE clauses and SELECT lists?
options: They are enforced by the warehouse itself at query time, so the policy holds even against a query nobody anticipated, rather than depending on every report author remembering to apply the restriction manually
They only work for queries written in a specific BI tool, not raw SQL
They require rewriting every existing report to add explicit filtering logic
They eliminate the need for any PII classification
mcqs.explanation: The whole value is that enforcement happens inside the warehouse's query engine regardless of who wrote the query or how, closing the gap that manual, per-report discipline can't reliably close. These mechanisms work across any SQL client, not just one BI tool, they don't require rewriting existing reports since the warehouse applies the policy transparently, and they depend on PII classification existing, not replace the need for it.

mcqs.question: A dataset has direct identifiers replaced with consistent artificial IDs, with a separate mapping table that can reverse the substitution. What technique is this, and is it equivalent to anonymization for compliance purposes?
options: This is pseudonymization, and it is not equivalent to anonymization — anyone with access to the mapping can still re-identify individuals
This is anonymization, and it fully satisfies any compliance requirement for irreversible de-identification
This is tokenization, and it is identical to anonymization in every respect
This is data minimization, which has nothing to do with identifiability
mcqs.explanation: Replacing identifiers with a consistent artificial ID while keeping a reversing mapping is exactly pseudonymization, and because the mapping makes reversal possible, treating it as equivalent to true anonymization is a common and real compliance mistake. It is not anonymization (which is meant to be irreversible), not tokenization (a related but distinct technique typically used for values like payment numbers with a secure vault), and unrelated to data minimization, which is about what's collected, not how identifiers are transformed.

mcqs.question: A dataset has names and emails removed and is labeled "de-identified," but still includes ZIP code, birth date, and gender. Why might this still be re-identifiable?
options: ZIP code, birth date, and gender are meaningless fields with no identifying power individually or in combination

The combination of these seemingly non-identifying fields can, in aggregate, narrow down to a specific individual when cross-referenced against other public data, even though no single field is an obvious direct identifier
Removing name and email always fully anonymizes a dataset regardless of what other fields remain
Re-identification is only possible if the original name and email are somehow recovered
mcqs.explanation: This is the well-documented finding behind the pitfall — a handful of individually unremarkable fields can jointly narrow down to one person when cross-referenced against other available data, which a naive "remove the obvious columns" checklist entirely misses. Removing name and email is not sufficient on its own, the fields in question are not meaningless, and re-identification here doesn't require recovering the original removed fields at all — that's precisely what makes it a subtle risk.

mcqs.question: Why does honoring a right-to-deletion request create real tension in a warehouse built around Type 2 SCD history and append-only storage?
options: Right-to-deletion requests are legally invalid for any warehouse using Type 2 SCD dimensions

The warehouse architecture is specifically designed to preserve every historical version and avoid overwriting data, which conflicts with surgically removing one person's data from every historical row without breaking downstream aggregates
Type 2 SCDs and append-only storage make it technically impossible to ever delete any data under any circumstances
Right-to-deletion only applies to streaming systems, not batch warehouses
mcqs.explanation: The tension is architectural — history-preserving, append-friendly designs exist specifically to avoid overwriting or losing data, which is in direct tension with a deletion request that needs to remove one person's data everywhere it appears without corrupting aggregates built on that history. Deletion is genuinely possible with the right approach (tombstoning, reprocessing), it isn't legally invalidated by the storage pattern, and the obligation applies to warehouses just as much as streaming systems.
